lead: Pressure in a static liquid increases with depth. A submerged gate, tank wall or dam face therefore carries a pressure that changes from point to point. Design needs one resultant force and the point where it acts, because a gate tips about a hinge or a dam overturns about its toe. For a plane surface the pressure distribution reduces to one resultant: F = p<sub>c</sub> A, where p<sub>c</sub> is the pressure at the centroid. The force acts at the centre of pressure, which lies below the centroid. This chapter also splits the force on a curved surface into a horizontal part from the projected area and a vertical part from the liquid weight.
prereq: You need: pressure variation with depth for p = ρgh, and manometer rules for same-level pressure.

blocks.text: Take a flat area A inside a liquid of density ρ. The free surface is the top liquid level. Let θ be the angle between the plane and the horizontal. Measure y along the plane from the free surface. A small strip at y has vertical depth h = y sin θ. Its pressure is p = ρ g h, so the force on it is dF = p dA.
F = ρ g h<sub>c</sub> A = p<sub>c</sub> A
blocks.where: F is total hydrostatic force in N; ρ is liquid density in kg/m³; g is gravitational acceleration, 9.81 m/s²; h<sub>c</sub> is vertical depth of the centroid of A in m; A is area in m²; p<sub>c</sub> is pressure at the centroid in Pa.

blocks.text: The centroid is the geometric centre of the area. The formula works because pressure varies linearly with depth, so the average pressure over A equals the pressure at the centroid.

The resultant does not act at the centroid. It acts at the centre of pressure, deeper than the centroid because lower strips carry more pressure. Along the plane, y<sub>cp</sub> = y<sub>c</sub> + I<sub>c</sub>/(A y<sub>c</sub>).

blocks.where: y<sub>cp</sub> is distance along the plane from the free surface to the centre of pressure in m; y<sub>c</sub> is distance along the plane to the centroid in m; I<sub>c</sub> is second moment of area about the centroidal axis parallel to the free surface in m⁴; A is area in m².

blocks.text: For a vertical rectangle with its top edge at the free surface, y<sub>c</sub> = h/2 and I<sub>c</sub> = b h³/12. Put them in the formula: y<sub>cp</sub> = h/2 + (b h³/12)/(b h × h/2) = 2h/3. The force acts at two-thirds of the height from the top.

The pressure prism is another picture. Plot pressure p = ρ g h normal to the surface. The volume of this prism equals the total force. Its centroid lies on the line of action. For a rectangle with top at the free surface, the pressure triangle has centroid at 2h/3 from the top.

A curved surface has pressure normal at every point, so the directions differ. Split the resultant into a horizontal component and a vertical component. Find each component by a simple rule, then combine them as vectors.

The horizontal component on a curved surface equals the force on the vertical projection of the surface. Project the curved area onto a vertical plane. Let A<sub>p</sub> be that projected area and h<sub>c</sub> its centroid depth. Then F<sub>H</sub> = ρ g h<sub>c</sub> A<sub>p</sub>. The line of action is the centre of pressure of the projected area.

blocks.where: F<sub>H</sub> is horizontal force component in N; A<sub>p</sub> is projected vertical area in m²; h<sub>c</sub> is vertical depth to the centroid of A<sub>p</sub> in m.

blocks.text: The vertical component equals the weight of the liquid that would stand above the curved surface up to the free surface. If liquid is below the surface, use an imaginary free surface. Let V be the volume between the surface and the free surface. Then F<sub>V</sub> = ρ g V. The line of action passes through the centroid of that volume.

blocks.where: F<sub>V</sub> is vertical force component in N; V is volume of liquid above the surface up to the free surface in m³.

blocks.text: Combine: F = √(F<sub>H</sub>² + F<sub>V</sub>²), and tan θ = F<sub>V</sub>/F<sub>H</sub>, where θ is the angle of the resultant to the horizontal. The line of action comes from the two components: F<sub>H</sub> acts at the centre of pressure of the projected vertical area, and F<sub>V</sub> acts through the centroid of the liquid volume between the surface and the free surface. Combine the two to locate the resultant. Liquid above pushes down; liquid below pushes up.

For a curved gate holding water, compute F<sub>H</sub> from the projected area and F<sub>V</sub> from the water volume above. Take moments about a hinge to find the opening force. This is the standard route for radial gates, tank ends and dam spillway crests.

figure.caption: The plane branch gives one force at the centre of pressure for the 2 m × 3 m gate; the curved branch shows the two component rules.

spec.aria: Hydrostatic force on a submerged gate splits into a plane-surface branch with force at the centre of pressure and a curved-surface branch with horizontal and vertical components.

examples.question: A vertical rectangular gate is 2 m wide and 3 m high. Its top edge is at the water free surface. Find the total hydrostatic force and the centre of pressure. Use ρ = 1000 kg/m³ and g = 9.81 m/s².
steps: Area A = b h = 2 m × 3 m = 6 m². Width b = 2 m, height h = 3 m.
Centroid depth h<sub>c</sub> = h/2 = 1.5 m because the top is at the free surface.
Pressure at centroid p<sub>c</sub> = ρ g h<sub>c</sub> = 1000 × 9.81 × 1.5 = 14,715 Pa.
Total force F = p<sub>c</sub> A = 14,715 × 6 = 88,290 N = 88.29 kN.
Second moment about centroidal axis parallel to free surface: I<sub>c</sub> = b h³/12 = 2 × 27 / 12 = 4.5 m⁴.
y<sub>c</sub> = h<sub>c</sub> = 1.5 m for a vertical gate. y<sub>cp</sub> = y<sub>c</sub> + I<sub>c</sub>/(A y<sub>c</sub>) = 1.5 + 4.5/(6 × 1.5) = 1.5 + 0.5 = 2.0 m from the top.
examples.answer: The total force is 88,290 N = 88.29 kN, acting at 2.0 m below the free surface, which is two-thirds of the gate height.
examples.check:
rho = 1000
g = 9.81
b = 2.0
h = 3.0
A = b * h
hc = h / 2.0
F = rho * g * hc * A
print(F)
print(F / 1000.0)
Ic = b * h**3 / 12.0
ycp = hc + Ic / (A * hc)
print(ycp)

traps: Using centroid depth h<sub>c</sub> as the centre of pressure. The force equals p<sub>c</sub> A, but it acts lower, at y<sub>cp</sub>.
Mixing y along an inclined plane with vertical depth h. Use h = y sin θ; the formula for y<sub>cp</sub> uses y, not h.
Using the wrong second moment. I<sub>c</sub> must be about the centroidal axis parallel to the free surface, not about the top edge or another axis.
Adding horizontal and vertical forces on a curved surface as plain numbers. They are perpendicular; combine by F = √(F<sub>H</sub>² + F<sub>V</sub>²).
Taking vertical force on a curved surface as weight of displaced volume. For hydrostatic force, use weight of liquid above the surface up to the free surface, real or imaginary.

quiz.a: The point on a submerged surface where the resultant hydrostatic force acts.

quiz.q: Write the plane-surface force formula and state what h<sub>c</sub> is.
quiz.a: F = ρg h<sub>c</sub> A; h<sub>c</sub> is the vertical depth of the centroid of the area.

quiz.q: Why is the centre of pressure below the centroid for a vertical plane with top at the free surface?
quiz.a: Pressure increases with depth, so lower strips carry larger force; the resultant shifts downward.

quiz.q: A vertical rectangular gate is 1.5 m wide and 4 m high. Its top edge is at the water free surface. Find the total force and the centre of pressure. Use ρ = 1000 kg/m³ and g = 9.81 m/s².
A curved surface has water above it. Why does horizontal force use projected area but vertical force use liquid weight?
quiz.a: Horizontal pressure components on the curved surface balance like pressure on its vertical projection. Vertical pressure components support the weight of the liquid column above the surface.

quiz.q: A vertical rectangular gate is 1 m wide and 2 m high. Its top edge is 1 m below the water free surface. Find the total force and the centre of pressure. Use ρ = 1000 kg/m³ and g = 9.81 m/s².
quiz.a: A = 1 × 2 = 2 m²; centroid depth h<sub>c</sub> = 1 + 1 = 2 m; F = 1000 × 9.81 × 2 × 2 = 39,240 N = 39.24 kN; I<sub>c</sub> = 1 × 2³/12 = 0.667 m⁴; y<sub>cp</sub> = 2 + 0.667/(2 × 2) = 2.167 m from the free surface.

quiz.q: For a plane area A at angle θ to the horizontal, h<sub>c</sub> = y<sub>c</sub> sin θ. A student uses y<sub>c</sub> in place of h<sub>c</sub> in F = ρg h<sub>c</sub> A. When is the error largest?
quiz.a: Largest when the plane is close to horizontal, because sin θ is small; there is no error at θ = 90°.

beyond: Not for the exam. Hydrostatic force calculations set the wall thickness of tanks, the hinge capacity of radial gates and the load on ship hulls. Designers use the same component rules in spreadsheets and in CFD models before adding waves and flow. Search for centre of pressure, hydrostatic force on a curved gate, and pressure prism.
